Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and impressions: Adult male with known type 2 diabetes and hypertension presenting with ~5 days of upper respiratory symptoms: dry hacking cough, rhinorrhea, myalgias, intermittent headache, chills and mild sore throat. Oropharyngeal exam shows mild posterior pharyngeal erythema, no tonsillar enlargement, no cervical lymphadenopathy; no respiratory distress, no wheeze reported. No vitals or investigations recorded. DDx analysis supports an infectious upper respiratory process and notes diabetes increases infection susceptibility.  
- Working diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold). Supported by symptom cluster (runny nose, sore throat, myalgias, dry cough), short duration (~5 days), and posterior pharyngeal erythema on exam (DDx: High likelihood).  
- Relevant differentials from DDx that refine assessment:  
  - Acute bronchitis — Medium likelihood: cough predominant and may follow URTI; considered if cough persists or worsens.  
  - ACE inhibitor (lisinopril)–induced cough — Low likelihood for current acute presentation given coexisting systemic viral symptoms, but plausible contributor if cough becomes chronic.  
- Considerations (additional plausible but uncertain options per DDx): Lower respiratory tract infection/pneumonia (Low likelihood presently given absence of dyspnea, focal chest signs or systemic toxicity). Allergic rhinitis/postnasal drip (Low–Medium) less likely given systemic symptoms.  
- Management plan documented in transcript: Symptomatic care only. Paracetamol already used. Clinician advised over-the-counter night/day cough preparations ("Night Nurse, Day Nurse") are acceptable with current medications. No antibiotic or other prescription issued. Return/seek review if any of the following: development of shortness of breath, wheeze, worsening symptoms, becoming systemically unwell, or symptoms persisting >3 weeks. Monitor blood glucose and blood pressure as usual.  
- Conflicts: None identified between transcript and DDx. If any future conflicting data arise, mark “conflict noted.”

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) — High. Classic symptom cluster (rhinorrhea, sore throat with posterior erythema, myalgias, headache) and short duration (~5 days) support this as the primary diagnosis.  
- Acute bronchitis — Medium. Predominant cough following URTI symptoms; consider if cough persists or becomes more severe.  
- ACE inhibitor (lisinopril)–induced cough — Low. Patient is on lisinopril, which can cause dry cough, but temporal features and systemic viral symptoms make this less likely as the primary cause of acute presentation; consider if cough becomes chronic.

- Internal conflicts or contradictions between transcript and DDx: None identified.
